content.summary_of_the_paper: This article proposes a new method for improving the isotropy of the distribution of CLS embeddings when fine-tuning transformers. The authors propose to insert one feed-forward layer between CLS embedding and the task-specific part of the model. First, the model is finetuned without this additional layer on down-stream tasks, and then this trainable layer is inserted, and everything else is frozen. When training this layer, a combination of losses is used - the old loss and the isotropic loss. This allows us to improve the work of Bert-base and Roberta-large on several tasks from GLUE by a few percent and also increase the isotropicity of embeddings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The method is simple, it really gives an increase of several percent on basic models.

Weaknesses:

- The authors test not non-SOTA models, if the approach is good, then why did they take not the recent approaches to evaluate it? Because of this, it is not clear whether it is now always necessary to do this and it will give a stably a few percents or not. Examples of superior models on GLUE include ERNIE and T5. 

- There is not enough comparison with training without this additional regularization loss. Suddenly, a simple increase in parameters due to the additional layer in itself gives an increase of 1-2 percent?

- Do not compare with whitening approaches and do not even cite this work, although it is very important
https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.15316

Other remarks:

- Typo in Table 2 in the last line

- The source code of the model is available on GitHub at (URL is not disclosed due to the double-blind review). And there it was definitely impossible to attach the code in the zip archive? There are questions about whether it is possible to reproduce

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a new method to enhance the text classification performance of fine-tuned PTLMs (i.e., BERT and RoBERTa). The authors introduced a feedforward layer for the [CLS] output vector and trained the feedforward layer with a task-specific loss and a newly proposed isotropic loss. The feedforward layer was placed between the PTLM and a task-specific layer. The isotropic loss was defined as the logarithmic inverse of the IsoScore. 

The experiment showed that the proposed method achieved higher performance in both classification tasks (3 tasks from GLUE) and the IsoScore. A comparison with a closely related baseline, IsoBN, revealed that the proposed method achieved similar performance in the classification tasks, and mixed results in the isotropic measure (explained variance).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. This paper proposed a simple method to improve text classification performance based on the recent finding on the isotropic behavior of the [CLS] output vectors.
2. The paper used the GLUE benchmark and the authors promised to public source code. Thus, the reproducibility is good.

Weaknesses
1. Since the analysis of the isotropy had already been done, the study in this paper could be considered incremental in terms of novelty. 
2. The comparison with IsoBN showed similar classification performance. While the authors noted that IsoBN trained the whole network and IsoLayer trained only one layer, it was unclear why the authors did not include an additional experiment where we had IsoLayer trained on the whole network.
3. The authors cited (Rajaee & Pilehvar, 2021b) for training only the IsoLayer to "maintain" the semantics. However, the logical step between the cited paper and the citing statement was unclear to me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the method could be considered novel, but the main findings were not new. The paper is clear enough and we can see the main motivation and why this is important. However, motivation for some design decisions could be more explicit, such as the choice to train only the IsoLayer, or empirically justified (moving average loss). In terms of quality, the authors can provide more experiment results (which are easy to perform) such as fine-tuning the whole network. And, the authors can have a deeper analysis between IsoLayer and other similar approaches (i.e, IsoBN).
content.summary_of_the_review: I am inclined toward rejecting this paper because of its incremental novelty in both technical and empirical aspects.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose the use of an Isotropy Layer after initial finetuning for a downstream task is performed in order to reduce anisotropy of output embeddngs used in classification. This Isotropy Layer is trained while the language model and downstream task layers are frozen using a novel joint loss function which is comprised of both the finetuning objective and the log of the inverse of the IsoScore, which measures the distance of the normalized covariance matrix of output representations and the identity matrix. The authors show that using the Isotropy Layer with the proposed loss improves downstream performance and the IsoScore on 3 GLUE datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The paper is well organized and easy to follow.
- The need to only finetune the Isotropy Layer while the other layers are frozen means that this approach can be applied retroactively to previously trained models.

Weaknesses

- The proposed method is quite similar in form to the IsoBN approach (Zhou, AAAI '21), other than performing this training after finetuning. Both methods seek to remove anisotropy in [CLS] representations by making gradient updates which tend outputs to be isotropic. 
- Performance for the proposed approach and IsoBN seems somewhat equivalent 
- More experiments (e.g. the rest of the GLUE task set) would be helpful
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work has clarity in the approach but originality is somewhat marginal (see weaknesses).
content.summary_of_the_review: In this paper, the authors propose an approach for enforcing isotropy in the output representations of language models for downstream tasks. Unlike previous methods, this approach can be applied after finetuning on a frozen model and task layer which reduces the number of parameters required for training. When using the proposed Isotropy Layer and composite loss function, performance gains of 2-3% are observed across 3 GLUE tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors tackle the issue of anisotropic embeddings that come out of Transformer models. Their approach is:

(1) Fit a fine-tuned model for the end task.
(2) Freeze the entire fine-tuned transformer.
(3) Put an intermediate isotropic layer in between the transformer and the task-specific head.
(4) Train the isotropic layer to end-task keep performance high but also increase isotropy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Thanks to the authors for the hard work on this paper. It is not ready for publication, in my opinion, but the core idea is interesting and is worth iterating on.

Strengths
------------
- Fixing isotropy seems like an interesting problem.
- Paper is pretty clear.
- The performance looks promising.

Weaknesses
----------------
- Claims made are often not experimentally validated, and they need to be. A few examples on page 5: "As we know, the fine-tuned model has learned some part of the knowledge... Freezing this fine-tuned model preserves the knowledge learned" - This claim has to be experimentally shown. Additional experiments would validate this. Similarly "...Therefore we freeze these layers to condition the output..." If you claim this to be true, you have to show it to be the case with experiments or theory. To be more clear, these claims are used to rule out experiments that are very natural: (1) frozen vs un-frozen transformer backbone and (2) frozen vs un-frozen fine-tuned head. But the claims aren't obviously true, so you need to try these variants to confirm that they are worse than the one fully-frozen variant you did experiment with.

- Elaborating on the weakness cited above, experimental design is too narrow in general. Page 6: "We selected the three specific datasets described in Table1" - Why? Use all of GLUE and add even more data on top of that to thoroughly validate this proposal. And there is no particular reason to limit to classification, is there? This is an empirical-only work. There are no datasets contributed, theory, user study, or other contributions. As such, the burden of empirical proof is high.

- Conclusion about the method's superiority are unwarranted. Page 7: "As we can see, our approach provides consistent improvements in both performance and isotropy." In Table 3, the IsoBN column is sometimes better than the IsoLayer column and the variances for both are generally larger than the difference between them. The differences don't look meaningful to me.

- Experimental design details are missing for unconvincing reasons. Page 9 claims the technical report is not available due to double-blind review. It can be added as an Appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: Promising idea, but needs a lot more experimental validation.

content.title: Optimizing the Performance of Text Classification Models by Improving the Isotropy of the Embeddings using a Joint Loss Function
content.abstract: Recent studies show that the spatial distribution of the sentence representations generated from pre-trained language models is highly anisotropic, meaning that the representations are not uniformly distributed among the directions of the embedding space. Thus, the expressiveness of the embedding space is limited, as the embeddings are less distinguishable and less diverse. This results in a degradation in the performance of the models on the downstream task. Most methods that define the state-of-the-art in this area proceed by improving the isotropy of the sentence embeddings by refining the corresponding contextual word representations, then deriving the sentence embeddings from these refined representations. In this study, we propose to improve the quality and distribution of the sentence embeddings extracted from the [CLS] token of the pre-trained language models by improving the isotropy of the embeddings. We add one feed-forward layer, referred to as the Isotropy Layer,  between the model and the downstream task layers. We train this layer using a novel joint loss function that optimizes an isotropy quality measure and the downstream task loss. This joint loss pushes the embeddings outputted by the Isotropy Layer to be more isotropic, and it also retains the semantics needed to perform the downstream task. The proposed approach results in transformed embeddings with better isotropy, that generalize better on the downstream task. Furthermore, the approach requires training one feed-forward layer, instead of retraining the whole network.  We quantify and evaluate the isotropy through multiple metrics, mainly the Explained Variance and the IsoScore. Experimental results on 3 GLUE datasets with classification as the downstream task show that our proposed method is on par with the state-of-the-art, as it achieves performance gains of around 2-3% on the downstream tasks compared to the baseline.
